title: Fictional fixture: allocating fuel for harbor night signals

period.label: 1880 harbor-board inquiry
period.note: The invented inquiry opens in 1880 and reports in 1881.

context.statement: Night signals depend on delivered lamp fuel and keeper labor.

actors.label: Fictional Harbor Signal Board
actors.role: Allocates the signal budget and issues the inquiry.

actors.label: Fictional Signal Keepers' Guild
actors.role: Argues that staffing and relighting time constrain coverage.

formulations.text: Which harbor entrances should receive a continuous night flame when the annual fuel allotment cannot supply every lamp?

vocabulary.meaning_in_context: A lamp kept lit from dusk to dawn by a staffed signal station.

institutions.label: Fictional Harbor Signal Board
institutions.role: Defines eligible entrances and distributes a fixed annual fuel allotment.

stakes.statement: Continuous coverage is treated as a navigation-safety benefit, while each additional station consumes scarce fuel and labor.

presuppositions.statement: A reliable night signal requires a locally tended flame and a recurring material supply.

accepted.statement: Give continuous flames to the busiest entrances and use scheduled flames elsewhere.

marginal.statement: Test passive reflective boards at minor entrances instead of staffed lamps.

unthinkable_or_impossible.statement: An unattended signal that can change itself in response to ship traffic is excluded as unavailable in the inquiry's own inventory of options.

answer_space.scope_note: The fixture records only options named or explicitly excluded in the invented inquiry; it does not infer every imaginable answer.

competing_formulations.text: How many stations can keepers safely tend without shortening relighting inspections?

sources.citation: Invented Harbor Signal Board, Minutes of the Fuel Inquiry (1880–1881).
sources.notes: Fictional calibration source; no historical claim is intended.

sources.citation: Invented Harbor Signal Board, Annual Fuel and Wage Ledger (1880).
Invented Signal Keepers' Guild, Petition on Night Coverage (1881).

evidence.excerpt: The inquiry shall sit from September 1880 and deliver its report before February 1881.
Which entrances shall retain a continuous night flame where the allotment cannot furnish every lamp?
evidence.interpretation: Supplies an explicit actor formulation and the scarcity constraint.

evidence.excerpt: The majority assigns full flame to the three busiest channels, scheduled lighting to the remainder, and a trial of reflector boards; no unattended changing apparatus is available to this board.
evidence.interpretation: Bounds the accepted, marginal, and explicitly unavailable answer space.

evidence.excerpt: Each station is itemized by oil deliveries, wick replacement, and keeper wages.
evidence.interpretation: Supports the episode's material and labor presuppositions.

evidence.excerpt: More lamps without more hands will shorten inspection rounds and delay every relighting after wind failure.

identity_claims.note: The later board calls its work the same signaling problem; this is preserved as an actor claim, not adopted automatically.
Institutional succession is visible, but the target, presuppositions, and answer space change.

continuity_evidence.note: The later institution explicitly claims continuity with the fuel-allocation inquiry.
Both disputes concern reliable night signaling at harbor entrances.

discontinuity_evidence.note: Local fuel and keeper labor cease to be the supply constraint in the networked episode.
Fuel schedules do not answer who may control automatic signal changes.

target_object.note: Harbor signals persist, but allocation of flames becomes authority over a network.

stakes.note: Safety remains, while procedural legitimacy becomes a new stake.

presuppositions.note: The later system no longer depends on fuel delivery to each signal.

answer_space.note: The earlier allocation answers are category-mismatched to the later control dispute.

historical_recognition.note: A direct retrospective claim exists, but it may be institutional self-narration.

askability.note: Remote control becomes askable only after networked signals replace locally tended flames.

answer_transfer.reasoning: Traffic-priority fuel schedules do not decide which body may issue automatic control rules.

presupposition_removal.reasoning: Removing local fuel consumption dissolves the earlier scarcity formulation.

historical_recognition.reasoning: The later board names a lineage, but the fixture supplies no independent transmission record.

relations.decision_note: The edge records historical succession without silently turning the later board's continuity claim into repository fact.

hindsight_risks.description: A modern reader may redescribe the inquiry as a generic automation problem.
hindsight_risks.mitigation: Keep the actor's fuel-allocation wording primary and treat automation only as an unavailable option explicitly named in the fixture.

uncertainties.description: The fictional surviving minutes may omit proposals made outside the board.
uncertainties.mitigation: Keep answer-space claims limited to the invented record set.
